notes.claim: A rectangle can be split into squares and counted, and the same area comes from multiplying width and height.
A triangle is half of a rectangle: its base and perpendicular height are the rectangle's width and height, so the area is half of base times height.
The base and perpendicular height of a triangle are at right angles to each other, so a sloping longest side is not used as the height.
Teachers watch for students who over-simplify to "add for perimeter" and "multiply for area", and who confuse the two ideas.
Shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas, which is how the confusion between the two is tackled.
Cutting a 2D shape up and rearranging it leaves its area unchanged, though not every child grasps this.

sources.title: How to work out an area - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: If you know the width and height of a rectangle, you can split it into squares and count them, to figure out its area.

sources.title: How to work out an area - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: You can also work out the area by multiplying the width and height together.

sources.title: Area - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: The area of the triangle is half the area of the rectangle.

sources.title: Area - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: The base of the triangle is the width of the rectangle and the perpendicular height of the triangle is equal to the height of the rectangle.

sources.title: Area of triangles - KS3 Maths - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: The base and the perpendicular height are at right angles to each other.

sources.title: Area of triangles - KS3 Maths - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: The longest side of 41 mm is not used because it is not at right angles to either of the other two sides.

sources.title: Area of triangles - KS3 Maths - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: This can be shown in diagrams and practically using paper and scissors.

sources.quote: The conservation of area means that if a 2D shape is cut up and rearranged, its area is unchanged. However, it has been shown that not all children grasp this.
